attempts.label: CRCNS:vta-2
attempts.entry_title: Dopamine cell firing in the bandit and Pavlovian tasks (Mohebi et al. 2019)
attempts.summary: The paper's findings on VTA dopamine cell firing mostly held up in this data, while its findings on dopamine release could not be tested, as the microdialysis and dLight recordings are not in the dataset. Latency tracked reward rate, and firing coded positive reward prediction errors and did not ramp before approach. Tonic firing changed little with reward rate, but some cells did change, and early-trial firing correlated with reward rate in 8 of 29 cells, which may come mostly from slow drift. Fewer cells responded to the light cue than reported, and the window and correction of the cue-response test are not given in the text read. Minor claims on cell identification and Pavlovian responses held in part.
attempts.description: Tests the dopamine cell findings of Mohebi, Pettibone, Hamid, Wong, Vinson, Patriarchi, Tian, Kennedy and Berke (2019) on CRCNS data set vta-2, which holds the spike times of the 29 optogenetically identified VTA-l dopamine cells with their bandit, Pavlovian and laser segments. It tests motivation and reward rate, the identification and firing rates of the cells, their Pavlovian responses, tonic firing across reward blocks, cue responses, approach ramps and reward prediction error coding. The microdialysis, photometry, histology and untagged units of the paper are not in the data set.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Mohebi et al. (2019) from CRCNS vta-2

outcomes.statement: Rats were more motivated when rewards were more likely; their latency from Light-On to Center-In scaled inversely with reward rate.
outcomes.source: Results, Dopamine tracks motivation in key loci, paragraph 1; Figure 1b
outcomes.quote: This was apparent in their “latency” – the time between Light-On and Center-In - which was sensitive to the outcome of the preceding few trials ( Extended Data Fig.1 ) and thereby scaled inversely with reward rate ( Fig.1b ).
outcomes.notes: 21 distinct bandit sessions (29 units; units of one session share identical events and are counted once), 6189 trials with a latency. Pearson r of the leaky-integrator reward rate at Light-On with log(latency) is negative in 21 of 21 sessions, mean -0.307 (one-sample t = -12.50, p = 6.6e-11), range -0.496 to -0.136; best tau 12 to 295 s, median 58 s, none at the grid's edge. Because tau is chosen to make r negative, a null was computed by repeating the choice of tau on latencies shuffled within the session (200 shuffles); 19 of 21 sessions have r below the null's 1st percentile. With one tau of 58 s for every session, r is negative in 21 of 21 (mean -0.291). The paper's statement covers its photometry and microdialysis rats too; only the electrophysiology sessions are in the data set.
deviations: Only the 21 electrophysiology bandit sessions are in the data set; the criterion names the photometry and microdialysis sessions as further readings where available.

A reward is counted at the rewarded Side-In, when the Results say the food hopper clicks; the Methods say only that reward rate is incremented each time a reward was received. A standard choice; no Light-On falls between Side-In and Food-Port-In.

Latency is Center-In minus Light-On from the event table, as the claims file defines it; the CNIlatency field is clipped at 65535 ms and not used. One trial with no latency (IM-1002_170118) is left out.
tau searched on a 1 s grid from 1 to 1200 s (Extended Data Fig. 1 legend gives the range); the shuffled-latency null uses 76 log-spaced values to keep the run short.

outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 1b
outcomes.quote: Top left, Regression analysis showing dependency of (log-) latency on the outcome of recent trials, during microdialysis sessions (n=26 sessions, 7113 trials, from 12 rats; error bars show SEM). Asterisks indicate average regression weights significantly different from zero (t-test, p<0.05).

outcomes.statement: Optogenetic tagging identified 27 well-isolated VTA-l cells with reliable short-latency light-evoked spikes as dopamine neurons, plus 2 retrogradely tagged cells from a rat with NAc core virus.
outcomes.source: Results, VTA firing is unrelated to motivation, paragraph 1 and paragraph 5; Methods, Electrophysiology, Classification
outcomes.quote: We found 27 well-isolated VTA-l cells with reliable short-latency spikes, and considered these identified dopamine neurons.
outcomes.notes: Only the 29 cells the paper selected are deposited, so the test is whether each passes the paper's criteria. SALT (Kvitsiani et al. 2013 defaults) on the 5 and 10 ms trains at 2 Hz gives p < 0.001 for 26 of the 27 VTA-l cells and both IM-1078 cells; none of the 29 passes with sham pulse times 250 ms later. IM1003170321t01c has p = 0.087 (5 ms) and 0.05 (10 ms), though p < 0.001 for two of its 1 ms trains. The correlation of the light-evoked with the session-wide waveform exceeds 0.9 for 23 of 27 VTA-l cells and 2 of 2 IM-1078 cells on the largest wire, and for 18 and 1 with the four wires concatenated, where the Methods say all light-evoked units exceeded 0.9. Cells meeting both criteria are 23 and 2 (largest wire, given as measured) or 18 and 1 (four wires); 23 is outside 27 +- 2.7, and 2 matches. By rat the data hold IM657 1, IM1002 3, IM1003 15, IM1037 8, IM-1078 2; the Methods give IM1037 9. Counting the two units with no 5 or 10 ms pulses as failing, instead of testing their 1 ms trains, gives 24 light-responsive VTA-l cells and 22 (largest wire) or 17 (four wires) passing both criteria; no reading brings the VTA-l total within tolerance.
deviations: The selection cannot be repeated from all recorded units, which are not deposited; only the deposited cells are tested against the criteria.

Units IM657160613t11a and IM1002170114t05b received no 5 or 10 ms pulses (their longest pulses are 1 ms, by the pulseWidth field); their 1 ms trains at 2 Hz are tested instead. This substitution is this attempt's choice, not the criterion's; counting both units as failing is shown and gives 22 (largest wire) and 17 (four wires).

SALT's baseline is the 400 ms before each pulse, with the test's published 10 ms window and 1 ms bins (claims file criterion); the baseline length is a standard choice. With 40 baseline windows the null has 780 distances, so the smallest nonzero p is 0.0013 and p < 0.001 means p = 0.
The waveforms are the deposited meanWave and meanLightEvoked; which wires the paper correlated is not given, and both readings are shown.

outcomes.statement: Identified dopamine neurons were tonically active with low firing rates, mean 7.7 Hz, range 3.7 to 12.9 Hz.
outcomes.source: Results, VTA firing is unrelated to motivation, paragraph 2; Figure 2d
outcomes.quote: All dopamine neurons were tonically-active, with relatively low firing rates (mean 7.7Hz; range 3.7–12.9Hz
outcomes.notes: Bandit-task rates (spikes between the first Light-On and the last Side-Out) of the 27 VTA-l cells have mean 7.77 Hz, minimum 3.77 and maximum 12.93 Hz, all within tolerance of 7.7, 3.7 and 12.9; the 29 cells give mean 7.72 Hz with the same range. Over all segments (bandit, Pavlovian, laser, sleep) the mean 7.41 and minimum 3.59 Hz match and the maximum 11.60 Hz does not. The descriptor's FR field gives 7.36, 3.62 and 11.73 Hz, within tolerance. Every cell fires throughout the task (ISI coefficient of variation 0.48 to 1.31).
deviations: The segment over which the session-wide rate is taken is not given; the bandit task (first reading in the criterion) matches, the whole recording matches for the mean and minimum only.

outcomes.source: Results, VTA firing is unrelated to motivation, paragraph 2; Figure 2d

outcomes.source: Results, VTA firing is unrelated to motivation, paragraph 2; Figure 2d
outcomes.quote: A distinct cluster of VTA-l neurons (n=38, from the same sessions) had brief waveforms, higher firing rates (>20Hz; mean 41.3Hz, range 20.1–97.1Hz), and included no tagged dopamine cells.
outcomes.notes: The data set holds only the 29 tagged dopamine cells (the Unit structure has 29 elements, all tagged); the untagged VTA-l units recorded in the same sessions are not deposited anywhere the paper names. None of the 38 non-dopamine cells is deposited.

outcomes.statement: In the Pavlovian task, dopamine cells responded strongly to randomly timed food hopper clicks and progressively less strongly when the clicks were made more predictable by preceding cues.
outcomes.source: Results, VTA firing is unrelated to motivation, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 5b,c
outcomes.quote: VTA-l dopamine cells responded strongly to randomly-timed food hopper clicks, and progressively less strongly when these clicks were made more predictable by preceding cues ( Extended Data Fig.5 ).
outcomes.notes: Peak spike density (20 ms SD) in the 0.5 s after the click, rewarded trials. Means over the 27 cells are unpredicted 47.3, medium 42.3, high 37.5 Hz, ordered as the claim states (50 ms bins 46.5, 41.8, 37.1; 29 cells 48.9, 43.9, 39.1), and 16 of 27 cells show the order individually. The per-cell one-way ANOVA has p < 0.05 in 12 of 27 cells (10 with 50 ms bins, 13 of 29), not more than half, so that part of the criterion fails. The data hold 8 VTA-l cells with 75/25% tones and 19 with 100/50%; 19 is within 18 +- 1.8 and 8 is outside 9 +- 0.9. The click times are the FoodDrop events, 3.136 s after trial onset. With the SD 4.5 ms kernel (the claims file's primary reading of variance 20 ms) the means are 112.6, 104.7 and 101.3 Hz, still ordered, and the ANOVA has p < 0.05 in 7 of 27. The tone-set count of 8 against 9 follows from the data holding 8 IM-1037 cells where the Methods give 9.
deviations: Peak firing read from the spike density with the 20 ms SD of the authors' getFiringRate.m as called by Fig5_replicate.m (the Methods say a Gaussian kernel with variance 20 ms, which the claims file reads as SD 4.5 ms); the SD 4.5 ms kernel and 50 ms bins are shown as variants and give the same outcome.

outcomes.statement: Dopamine cell responses to the Pavlovian cues followed the cues' reward probability, in line with RPE-like coding.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 5b,c; Results, VTA firing is unrelated to motivation, paragraph 3
outcomes.inferred: The Results say only that the Pavlovian responses are consistent with canonical RPE-like coding; the cue part is read from the Extended Data Fig. 5 legend, which plots and tests the cue response by tone. The figure was not seen.
outcomes.notes: Peak spike density in the 0.5 s after cue onset. Means over the 27 cells are zero 29.6, medium 31.8, high 36.3 Hz, ordered as the claim states in both tone sets (100/50/0: 30.8, 33.0, 36.8; 75/25/0: 26.7, 29.0, 35.1), and 16 of 27 cells show the order individually. The per-cell ANOVA has p < 0.05 in 10 of 27 (11 of 29), not more than half. With the SD 4.5 ms kernel the means are 94.1, 95.8 and 101.3 Hz, still ordered, and the ANOVA has p < 0.05 in 4 of 27.
deviations: Peak firing read from the spike density with the 20 ms SD of the authors' getFiringRate.m; the SD 4.5 ms kernel of the claims file's primary reading is shown and gives the same outcome (see ed5-pavlovian-dopamine-click-responses).

outcomes.statement: Rats learned the cue probabilities; in an example session the rat entered the food port more during the 75% cue than the 25% and 0% cues.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 5a legend
outcomes.quote: This rat was more likely to go to the food port during the cue that was highly (75%) predictive of rewards compared to the other cues (25% and 0%; one-way ANOVA, F=11.1, p<1.2×10 −6 ).

statistics.about: food-port head entry during 0.3 to 3 s after cue onset, across the three cues, one session

outcomes.notes: Seven distinct sessions with 75/25/0% tones (IM-1037 and IM-1078). Fraction of 0.3 to 3 s after cue onset at the food port, one-way ANOVA across the three tones per session: the 75% cue is highest with p < 0.05 in 5 of 7 sessions, all 5 with p < 1.2e-6 (largest F 55.6, smallest p 1.1e-17); whether the rat entered the port at any time in the epoch gives the same counts (largest F 76.6). In the 14 sessions with 100/50/0% tones the high cue is highest in 11 but p < 0.05 in only 2 (fraction) or 5 (any entry).
deviations: The food-port status (portStatus) is taken as aligned on trial onset from 2 s before to 10 s after (its Win field), at 30 kHz (360000 samples over 12 s); neither is documented, and occupancy rising after the click on unpredicted trials is consistent with it. Kept at 1 kHz.

outcomes.statement: Tonic dopamine cell firing in each block was indifferent to reward rate, with no significant change in the firing rate of any individual dopamine cell between higher- and lower-reward blocks.
outcomes.source: Results, VTA firing is unrelated to motivation, paragraph 4; Figure 2e-h
outcomes.quote: However, in the bandit task tonic dopamine cell firing in each block of trials was strikingly indifferent to reward rate ( Fig.2e , g ). There was no significant change in the firing rates of individual dopamine cells
outcomes.notes: Blocks split per session at the median of block-mean reward rate (high blocks have a mean reward rate 2.10 rewards higher on the integrator's scale). The two readings disagree. Reading (b), rank-sum of block-mean rates: 2 of 27 cells differ at p < 0.05 with the median block dropped, 0 with it put low (binomial p = 0.394 for 2 of 27). The 6 cells with 2 blocks a side cannot reach p < 0.05 even with complete separation (smallest p 0.121), and the 6 with 3 a side only just can (0.0495), so this reading has little power; 2 of the 21 cells that can reach p < 0.05 do. Reading (a), rank-sum of 1 min bin rates: 18 of 27 cells differ (19 with the median block put low), against 1.35 expected (binomial p = 1.2e-17); regressing bin rates on block type and time in session, 16 of 27; against circular shifts of the bins' high/low labels, which keep the bins' serial dependence, 9 of 27 (7 with the median block put low; binomial p = 4.0e-6). Across cells firing is higher in high-reward blocks by a median 0.50 Hz (range -0.63 to 1.38 Hz; signed-rank p = 0.0006). Tonic firing changes little, about 0.5 Hz on a mean near 7.7 Hz, as the paper describes, but individual cells change under the tests on 1 min bins, where the claim says none did; reading (b) finds no more cells than chance, with little power. The question of the test is put to the authors (findings).
deviations: The test of Fig. 2f is in the unread legend; the claims file names two readings, both run. Reading (a) is also run against circular shifts of the high/low labels of the 1 min bins (shifts of 10 or more bins), because the bins are not independent; the minimum shift is a standard choice.
With an odd number of blocks the median block is dropped (a standard choice); putting it with the low blocks is shown as a variant.
1 min bins are laid from the session's first Light-On, and a bin counts for a block when it lies wholly inside it; block limits run from a block's first attempt to the next block's first attempt.

outcomes.statement: No other VTA-l neurons changed firing rate between higher- and lower-reward blocks.
outcomes.source: Results, VTA firing is unrelated to motivation, paragraph 4; Figure 2f,h
outcomes.quote: There was no significant change in the firing rates of individual dopamine cells – or any other VTA-l neurons - between higher- and lower-reward blocks
outcomes.notes: The data set holds only the 29 tagged dopamine cells (the Unit structure has 29 elements, all tagged); the untagged VTA-l units recorded in the same sessions are not deposited anywhere the paper names. The claim is on the 38 non-dopamine and other VTA-l units.

outcomes.statement: There was no overall change in the rate at which dopamine cells fired bursts between higher- and lower-reward blocks.
outcomes.source: Results, VTA firing is unrelated to motivation, paragraph 4; Figure 2i
outcomes.quote: There was also no overall change in the rate at which dopamine cells fire bursts of spikes ( Fig.2i ).
outcomes.notes: Bursts by the 80/160 ms template, per minute in high and low blocks for the 27 VTA-l cells (medians 60.5 and 61.0 bursts/min). High minus low median 1.28 bursts/min, range -12.4 to 17.7; Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 0.645, paired t p = 0.491. With the median block put low p = 0.714 and 0.549; with 29 cells Wilcoxon p = 0.536.
deviations: The population test is in the unread Fig. 2 legend; both readings the criterion names agree.

outcomes.statement: Dopamine cells never switched between active and inactive states; the proportion of time spent inactive (long inter-spike intervals) was very low and did not change between higher- and lower-reward blocks.
outcomes.source: Results, VTA firing is unrelated to motivation, paragraph 4; Figure 2i
outcomes.quote: The proportion of time dopamine cells spent inactive (long inter-spike-intervals) was very low, and did not change between higher- and lower-reward blocks ( Fig.2i ).
outcomes.notes: Share of bandit-task time in inter-spike intervals longer than 0.5, 1 and 2 s, median over the 27 cells 4.7%, 0.13% and 0% (maximum 46.2%, 18.1% and 2.4%), below the 5% read as very low. High against low blocks the medians differ by -0.02, 0 and 0 percentage points; Wilcoxon p 0.551, 0.356, 0.463; paired t p 0.637, 0.166, 0.382. At 0.5 s the median (4.7%) is close to the 5% bound. The statement that no cell switched between active and inactive states is not quantified by the criterion.
deviations: The long-ISI threshold and the 5% bound are readings in the claims file, not from the paper; all three thresholds agree.

outcomes.statement: Retrograde CTb from NAc core labelled TH+ neurons in the VTA-l recording zone, where 21% of TH+ cells were also CTb+.
outcomes.source: Results, VTA firing is unrelated to motivation, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 3

outcomes.statement: The two retrogradely tagged VTA-l dopamine cells, infected from NAc core, had firing patterns closely resembling the other tagged cells, including no tonic firing change with reward rate.
outcomes.source: Results, VTA firing is unrelated to motivation, paragraph 5; Supplementary Figure (last two pages)
outcomes.quote: Both retrogradely-infected cells had firing patterns that closely resembled the other tagged dopamine cells in all respects, including lack of tonic firing changes with varying reward rate ( Supplementary Figure ).
outcomes.notes: The two IM-1078 cells fire at 7.85 and 6.17 Hz in the bandit task (7.90 and 6.22 over all segments), inside 3.33 to 14.19 Hz. Under reading (b) of the tonic test neither differs (p = 0.076 and 0.75), and with 5 or 6 blocks a side that test could reach p = 0.009 and 0.004. Reading (a) against circular shifts of the labels also finds no change (p = 0.27 and 0.85). The plain rank-sum of 1 min bins finds a change in IM1078180827t14a (0.67 Hz higher in high blocks, p = 5.8e-5), but it treats serially dependent bins as independent. Their event responses lie within the range of the 27 cells (peak after rewarded Side-In 27.8 and 17.6 Hz against 8.4 to 45.8; Light-On peak 18.5 and 14.0 against 6.5 to 18.5).
deviations: Assumed: the per-cell tonic test is one that has power for these cells and allows for serial dependence, reading (b) or reading (a) against circular shifts; both find no change. The plain rank-sum of 1 min bins (reading a as written) finds a change in one cell and is set aside because its bins are not independent (fig2efgh-tonic-firing-indifferent-to-reward-rate).

outcomes.statement: Light-On, the Go cue and rewarded Side-In (food hopper click) each evoked a rapid firing increase in dopamine cells, seen in the great majority of cells.
outcomes.source: Results, Dopamine firing does not explain release, paragraph 1; Figure 4a,c
outcomes.quote: External stimuli at Light-On, Go cue, and rewarded Side-In (food hopper click) each evoked a rapid firing increase ( Fig.4a ). These responses were observed in the great majority of dopamine cells ( Fig.4c )
outcomes.notes: Time-to-cue-response shuffle test (40 ms bins in 20 ms steps, 10,000 paired shuffles against the 250 ms before the event, p < 0.01 Bonferroni over the bins). With the 0.5 s window: Go cue 27 of 27, rewarded Side-In 24 of 27, Light-On 16 of 27 (59%), so two events reach the 75% read as a great majority and Light-On exceeds half only. With the 1 s window: 27, 25 and 13 of 27 (Light-On 48%). Without the correction 22 of 27 respond to Light-On (0.5 s window). With events shifted 5 s earlier no cell responds. Median first significant bin 0.12 s (Light-On), 0.04 s (Go), 0.06 s (Side-In). On trials with latency over 0.5 s only, so that no Center-In falls in the 0.5 s window, 11 of 27 respond to Light-On (median 258 of 298 trials kept), so leaving Center-In out of the window does not bring the count nearer the 75% bar.
deviations: The post-cue window over which bins are tested is not given. Assumed: 0.5 s, because the Methods' test looks for the first significant bin after a cue and the responses are described as rapid; the 1 s window (Bonferroni over 49 bins) is shown and gives the same outcome for the Go cue and Side-In, and under half of the cells for Light-On.

What the shuffle exchanges is not given; here it swaps, trial by trial, the post-cue bin rate and the baseline rate (a paired permutation). The correction is read as Bonferroni over the bins tested (claims file header).

outcomes.quote: The NAc dLight signal also responded rapidly and reliably to each of these salient cues ( Fig.4b , c )

outcomes.source: Results, Dopamine firing does not explain release, paragraph 2 and paragraph 3; Figure 4a,f
outcomes.quote: However, the VTA-l dopamine cell population did not show a corresponding increase in firing at these times ( Fig.4a
outcomes.notes: Ramp angle from the 50 ms smoothed mean rate in the 0.5 s before the event. Before Center-In on trials with latency over 2 s the angle is positive in 7 of 27 cells (one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.991, sign test p = 0.997); before Food-Port-In on rewarded trials in 12 of 27 (p = 0.411 and 0.779). With 29 cells the same (p 0.56 to 0.999). The angles are near +-90 degrees because time and rate keep their own units; the sign decides.
deviations: The 50 ms Gaussian kernel is read as its SD. The test of Fig. 4f is in the unread legend; both readings the criterion names agree.

outcomes.statement: NAc dLight increased before Center-In on long-latency trials in 10 of 10 sessions and before Food-Port-In in 9 of 10, distinct from cue-evoked release and without corresponding increases in dopamine firing.
outcomes.source: Results, Dopamine firing does not explain release, paragraph 3; Figure 4d-f
outcomes.quote: dLight signals consistently increased before Center-In on long-latency trials (10/10 sessions), and also before Food-Port-In (9/10 sessions), without corresponding increases in dopamine firing ( Fig.4f ).
outcomes.notes: The data set has no photometry (dLight) recordings; it holds only spike times of the 29 tagged dopamine cells and their behaviour (vta-2/live/data_and_code.zip). The paper names no other archive for them.

outcomes.statement: Dopamine cell firing increases were locked to Light-On, preferentially on short-latency trials; all 25 cells with significant increases after Light-On were better aligned to Light-On than to Center-In.
outcomes.source: Results, Dopamine firing does not explain release, paragraph 3; Figure 4d,e
outcomes.quote: Increases in dopamine cell firing were consistently locked to the cue onset at Light-On, preferentially for short-latency trials. All 25 dopamine cells with significant firing rate increases after Light-On were better aligned to Light-On than Center-In ( Fig.4e ).
outcomes.notes: 16 of 27 cells have a significant increase after Light-On by the shuffle test (0.5 s window; 13 with the 1 s window, 11 on trials with latency over 0.5 s), against 25 +- 2.5. Of the 16, 15 have a higher trial-averaged peak (within 0.5 s of the event) aligned on Light-On than on Center-In (reading a; 14 with the SD 4.5 ms kernel), and 5 a smaller trial-to-trial SD of the response peak time relative to Light-On (reading b); neither reading gives all of them. The Light-On response (peak in 0.5 s) is larger on short-latency (< 1 s) than long-latency (> 2 s) trials in 22 of 27 cells, median 6.70 Hz, Wilcoxon p = 8.4e-5. The preference for short-latency trials holds; the count and the all-cells part of the criterion fail.
deviations: The shuffle test's window is assumed as in fig4ac-dopamine-cue-responses; the 1 s window gives 13 cells, so the count fails either way.
Reading (b) is implemented as the time of the per-trial spike density maximum between Light-On and 0.5 s after Center-In, on trials with latency under 5 s.

outcomes.statement: During the early part of each trial dopamine cell firing did not depend on reward rate, though reward rate affected motivation.
outcomes.source: Results, Dopamine firing does not explain release, paragraph 4; Figure 5a,b
outcomes.quote: During the early part of each trial dopamine cell firing was not dependent on reward rate ( Fig.5a ) - despite the influence of reward rate on motivation ( Fig.5b ).
outcomes.notes: 29 cells. Firing in the 0.5 s after Light-On correlates with reward rate at p < 0.01 in 8 cells (7 positive), against 1% by chance (binomial p = 3.6e-10); in the 0.5 s before Center-In in 6 cells (4 positive; p = 3.9e-7). The population Friedman test across reward-rate terciles finds no dependence (p = 0.080 and 0.19); tercile means after Light-On are 8.53, 8.76 and 8.92 Hz. With the 27 cells, 8 and 6 cells (binomial p = 1.9e-10 and 2.5e-7) and Friedman p = 0.20 and 0.32. The criterion requires neither test to show a dependence; the per-cell count does, with firing mostly higher at higher reward rate. The second part of the statement (reward rate affects motivation) is fig1b, reproduced. Against circular shifts of reward rate over trials (shifts of 20 or more trials), which keep the serial dependence the Pearson p-values ignore, 1 and 2 of 29 cells are significant (binomial p = 0.25 and 0.034), so most of the per-cell count may come from slow drift shared by firing and reward rate; the outcome follows the criterion's Pearson test.
deviations: The windows and test of Fig. 5a are in the unread legend; the claims file names the readings, all run.
The circular-shift null is a variant added at the verifier's request; the minimum shift of 20 trials is a standard choice.

outcomes.statement: The phasic dopamine response to the reward cue at Side-In was reliably stronger when reward rate was lower, consistent with positive RPE coding, strongly and consistently across cells.
outcomes.source: Results, Dopamine firing does not explain release, paragraph 4; Figure 5a; Extended Data Fig. 8
outcomes.quote: Subsequently, the phasic response to the reward cue was reliably stronger when reward rate was lower ( Fig.5a ), consistent with positive RPE encoding.
outcomes.notes: Peak spike density in the 250 ms after rewarded Side-In against reward rate at Side-In (before the trial's reward). Tercile means 38.2, 31.4, 28.2 Hz from low to high reward rate; median Pearson r -0.310 (Wilcoxon p = 3.7e-8); significant negative correlations 21 and positive 0 before correction, 17 and 0 after Bonferroni over 29. Spearman: 20 and 0; 27 cells: 20 and 0; SD 4.5 ms kernel: 13 and 0 (tercile means 104.4, 95.9, 91.4 Hz). Median r by rat -0.17 (IM-1078) to -0.41 (IM-1002).
deviations: The kernel SD is 20 ms, from the authors' getFiringRate.m as called by Fig5_replicate.m (twsize = 0.02 is the normpdf sigma); the literal reading of the Methods (variance 20 ms^2, SD 4.5 ms) is shown and agrees.

outcomes.statement: When the reward cue was omitted dopamine cells paused, but encoding of negative RPEs was much weaker or absent, at the population level and in individual cells; negative RPE coding by pause duration was seen in only 2 of 29 neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Dopamine firing does not explain release, paragraph 4; Figure 5a,b; Extended Data Fig. 8
outcomes.quote: When this reward cue was omitted dopamine cells paused firing, though encoding of negative RPEs was much weaker or absent... It has been proposed that negative RPEs are encoded in the duration of dopamine pauses 31 , but this was observed in just 2/29 individual neurons.
outcomes.notes: Unrewarded trials, pause in the 2 s after Side-In under three readings. Counting the window's bounds as boundaries, 8 of 29 cells lengthen their pause significantly with reward rate (5 after Bonferroni correction); with whole inter-spike intervals overlapping the window, 9 and 5; with only intervals between spikes inside the window, 2 and 2, which drops 50 of 3695 trials (38 in one cell). Only the last matches the paper's 2/29. Under every reading fewer cells code negative RPE by the pause than code positive RPE by the peak (21 before, 17 after correction). The valley part cannot be tested: the minimum of the 20 ms spike density is under 0.5 Hz on 3694 of 3695 unrewarded trials in the 1 to 3 s window (the largest 0.91 Hz) and on all 3695 in the 0 to 2 s window, and the same on every trial in 21 (1 to 3 s) and 27 (0 to 2 s) of the 29 cells, and in all 29 with the SD 4.5 ms kernel. A valley correlation is defined only for 8 and 2 cells, none of them significant, and the comparison with the peak holds by construction. The authors' Fig5_replicate.m computes neither the valley nor the pause. Population pause by tercile 0.49, 0.52, 0.55 s (Friedman p = 9.7e-5, bounds reading). Measured is the bounds reading before correction.
deviations: How the pause is measured at the window's edges is not given (Extended Data Fig. 8 legend, maximum inter-spike interval within 2 s after unrewarded Side-In); three readings are run and they disagree, so the outcome is partial and rests on no single one.

The valley uses the 20 ms SD kernel of the authors' code, and the SD 4.5 ms kernel as a variant; with either the minimum is 0 Hz on nearly every trial. The paper does not say how its valley avoided this, and the authors' code in the data set does not compute it.
Correction for the 2/29 count is read both ways (before and after Bonferroni over 29).

outcomes.statement: Similar dopamine firing results held when reward expectation was estimated by trial-based actor-critic or Q-learning models or by counting recent rewards.
outcomes.source: Results, Dopamine firing does not explain release, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 8
outcomes.quote: Similar results were obtained if reward expectation was estimated in other ways, including trial-based reinforcement learning models (actor-critic, Q-learning) or simply counting recent rewards ( Extended Data Fig.8 ).
outcomes.notes: Alpha per session by the most negative correlation with log latency (0.01 to 1; it reaches 1 in 2 sessions for the actor-critic and 4 for Q-learning, and 0.01 in 1 for Q-learning; the fit is weak under both models in IM-1003_170404 and IM-1037_180112, r -0.165 and -0.035 for the actor-critic, -0.167 and 0.016 for Q-learning, and good in the other two Q-learning sessions at 1.00, r -0.346 and -0.402). Rewards in the last 10 trials: tercile means 38.7, 31.7, 29.0 Hz, median r -0.321, 20 cells negative and 0 positive (18 after correction); actor-critic V: 38.5, 31.2, 28.5 Hz, median r -0.312, 23 and 0 (17); Q-learning Q_left + Q_right: 38.2, 29.8, 30.1 Hz, median r -0.215 (Wilcoxon p = 1.1e-8), 16 and 0 (12). The fig5a criteria hold for the first two estimates; for Q-learning the middle tercile is 0.3 Hz below the highest. Negative coding by the pause is weaker under all three: 2, 2, 2 pause cells (interval reading), 8, 6, 4 (bounds reading), 6, 6, 6 (whole-ISI reading) against 20, 23, 16 peak cells. No valley cell is significant, but the valley is degenerate (fig5ab-weak-negative-rpe), so that part holds by construction.
deviations: Initial values 0.5 and the alpha range 0.01 to 1 are the claims file's readings; the fit measure is the most negative correlation with log latency, as for tau.
Rewards in the last 10 trials are counted as in the authors' pelletpermin.m (fewer trials at the start of a session).
Pause and valley measured as in fig5ab-weak-negative-rpe, with its three pause readings.

outcomes.statement: NAc dLight at Side-In showed a transient encoding of positive but not negative RPEs, slightly delayed and prolonged compared to firing but subsecond.
outcomes.source: Results, Dopamine firing does not explain release, paragraph 5; Figure 5c,d
outcomes.quote: Dopamine release at Side-In also showed a clear, transient encoding of positive, but not negative, RPEs ( Fig.5c , d ). This dLight response was slightly delayed and prolonged compared to firing, consistent with time taken for release and reuptake 32 , but remained a subsecond phenomenon.
outcomes.notes: The data set has no photometry (dLight) recordings; it holds only spike times of the 29 tagged dopamine cells and their behaviour (vta-2/live/data_and_code.zip). The paper names no other archive for them.

outcomes.statement: Unlike firing, dLight early in each trial was greater when recent trials had been rewarded, even while the rat held still in the center port awaiting the Go cue.
outcomes.source: Results, Dopamine firing does not explain release, paragraph 5; Figure 5c,d
outcomes.quote: Unlike firing, however, dLight signals early in each trial were greater when recent trials had been rewarded ( Fig.5c ), consistent with value coding. We observed this dependence on reward history even while the rat was not actively moving, but was maintaining a nosepoke in the center port waiting for the Go cue ( Fig.5d ).
outcomes.notes: The data set has no photometry (dLight) recordings; it holds only spike times of the 29 tagged dopamine cells and their behaviour (vta-2/live/data_and_code.zip). The paper names no other archive for them.

outcomes.statement: Rapid behaviour-linked dLight fluorescence changes occur with 470 nm excitation and not in the 405 nm control band.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 7 legend
outcomes.quote: Rapid, behavior-linked dLight fluorescence changes occur at 470nm, as expected, not in the control 405nm band.
outcomes.notes: The data set has no photometry (dLight) recordings; it holds only spike times of the 29 tagged dopamine cells and their behaviour (vta-2/live/data_and_code.zip). The paper names no other archive for them.

outcomes.statement: Non-dopamine cell firing was more variable but on average showed activity during movements, starting just before Center-In regardless of latency, before Side-In and before Food-Port-In.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 7 legend
outcomes.quote: Non-dopamine cell firing is much more variable (wider error bands), but on average shows activity during movements... starting just before Center-In (irrespective of latency), just before Side-In , and just before Food-Port-In .
outcomes.notes: The data set holds only the 29 tagged dopamine cells (the Unit structure has 29 elements, all tagged); the untagged VTA-l units recorded in the same sessions are not deposited anywhere the paper names. The claim is on the 38 non-dopamine cells.

findings.statement: The data set holds only the spike times and behaviour of the 29 tagged dopamine cells. The paper's microdialysis (26 sessions, 12 rats), dLight photometry (10 sessions), in vitro dLight imaging, CTb histology and the untagged VTA-l units recorded with the tagged cells (including the 38 non-dopamine cells) are not in it, though the paper says all data will be available through CRCNS. 20 of the 37 claims cannot be tested.
The data description says the 29 cells were recorded from 4 rats; they come from 5 (IM-657 1, IM-1002 3, IM-1003 15, IM-1037 8, IM-1078 2), the last being the rat with NAc core virus.

The CNIlatency field ("latency to center-nose-in", ms) is stored as 65535 for every latency above 65.535 s (120 trials in 19 of 21 sessions), the largest 16-bit integer; and in 4 sessions one value differs from Center-In minus Light-On by more than 5 ms (in IM-657_160613 the last trial repeats the previous trial's value). ReactionTime also differs from Center-Out minus Go cue by up to 273 ms in 3 sessions.
Spike times are not in ascending order in at least one segment of 11 of the 29 units (inversions of at most 0.7 ms, for example 2399.4923 s after 2399.4926 s in the RL segment of IM657160613t11a).

The Methods give the tagged cells per rat as IM657 1, IM1002 3, IM1003 15 and IM1037 9, which sums to 28, while the text says 27 VTA-l cells. The data hold 8 IM1037 cells (27 in all). Extended Data Fig. 5b gives 9 cells with 75/25% Pavlovian tones and 18 with 100/50%; the data hold 8 and 19, the IM657 cell having 100/50% tones.

Several fields are not described. The FR field ("session-wide average firing rate") matches none of the rates computable from the segments (it differs from the bandit-task rate by up to 1.95 Hz). The seven rows of the bandit event table are named only in Fig5_replicate.m, and the two rows of the Pavlovian one not at all. The Pavlovian portStatus window (Win, -2 to 10 s) does not say what it is aligned to, nor its 30 kHz sampling. meanWave and meanLightEvoked have no units or sampling rate.

Against the Methods' identification criteria: the deposited light-evoked and session-wide mean waveforms correlate below 0.9 for 4 of the 27 VTA-l cells on the largest wire (9 with the four wires), where the Methods say all light-evoked units exceeded 0.9; units IM657160613t11a and IM1002170114t05b received no 5 or 10 ms pulses, where the Methods require p < 0.001 for 5 and 10 ms trains; and IM1003170321t01c is not significant by SALT with its 5 and 10 ms trains (p = 0.087 and 0.05), though it is with 1 ms trains.

The authors' script in the data set (Fig5_replicate.m) splits trials by the number of rewards in the previous 10 trials into four groups (0-2, 3-5, 6-7, 8-10), while Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 8 use terciles of the leaky-integrator reward rate. Its Gaussian kernel has SD 20 ms (getFiringRate.m, sigma = twsize = 0.02), where the Methods say variance 20 ms.

Question for the authors on Fig. 2f,h: which per-cell test compared tonic firing between high- and low-reward blocks, and on what samples (1 min bins, as the Methods count tonic spikes, or block means), and how was the median block handled with an odd number of blocks? With rank-sum tests on 1 min bins 18 of 27 cells differ (p < 0.05), 9 against circular shifts of the block labels, and firing is higher in high-reward blocks by a median 0.50 Hz; with block means 2 (or 0) cells differ, but 6 of 27 cells have too few blocks for that test to reach p < 0.05.

Question for the authors on the time-to-cue-response test (Methods, Analysis, paragraph 1, and Fig. 4c,e): what was shuffled, how was the correction for multiple comparisons made, and over what post-cue window? With paired shuffles and Bonferroni over the bins of a 0.5 s window, 16 of 27 cells respond to Light-On (13 with 1 s, 22 without correction), where the paper reports 25. This attempt adopted the 0.5 s window.

Question for the authors on Extended Data Fig. 8: is the pause the longest interval between spikes within the 2 s after unrewarded Side-In, does it include the intervals to the window's bounds, or is it the longest whole inter-spike interval overlapping the window, and what smoothing gave the valley? Intervals between spikes only give the paper's 2/29 pause cells; counting the bounds gives 8 (5 after correction) and whole intervals 9 (5). With the 20 ms kernel, or the 4.5 ms one, the valley is 0 Hz on nearly every unrewarded trial, so it cannot correlate with reward rate. The data set's Fig5_replicate.m computes neither.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper modules and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier listed the archive itself (bucket listing, filelist.txt, checksums.md5) and tested vta.salt, vta.bursts, cue_response and the valley on synthetic spike trains. It agreed with 33 of 37 outcomes and gave a different outcome for fig2efgh, retro, fig4e and fig5ab; all four were changed to the verifier's. It reported no place where the claims file misreads the paper, so no question was added for a reader. Report in transcripts/mohebi-2019/verifier-1-report.md.

disagreements.reason: Reading (a), the 1 min bins, finds 18 or 19 of 27 cells significant. Reading (b), the block means, finds 2 of 27 or 0 of 27, but that test has almost no power: with 2 against 2 blocks a rank-sum test cannot go below p = 0.12, and with 3 against 3 its minimum is 0.0495, so the 7 IM-1037 cells and 6 others had a guaranteed no change, and the 0 of 27 cannot be read as absence of an effect. Reading (a) treats autocorrelated 1 min bins as independent and is anticonservative; the variant that adds a time regressor still gives 16 of 27. The across-cell signed-rank test (p = 6e-4, high blocks a median +0.5 Hz above low) is the sound test here, and it shows a change.

Reading (b): neither cell changes (p = 0.076 and 0.75), and here 5 or 6 blocks per side give the test real power; both rates are in range. Under reading (a), IM1078180827t14a is significant (p = 5.8e-5).

16 cells respond to Light-On against the expected 25 +- 2.5 (22 even without correction). Under reading (a), 15 of 16 are better aligned to Light-On, not all. The short-versus-long latency part holds: 22 of 27 cells, p = 8e-5. Item 3: the Light-On peaks and alignment were run under SD 20 ms only.

The pause count is 2 of 29 only under the ISI-only reading; the window-edge reading gives 8 (5 after correction). The ISI-only reading drops trials with fewer than 2 spikes, the longest pauses, which biases it toward no correlation; the edge reading counts the silence from Side-In to the first spike, which is part of a pause. The valley part is never really tested, because the valley is 0 Hz on 100% of 3695 trials, so the criterion's fewer valley than peak cells holds by construction; Fig5_replicate.m was not consulted for how the minimum is computed. Population pause duration rises with reward rate (Friedman p = 9.7e-5).

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook with the conclusions and summary, the helper modules, the README, the attempt record and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier agreed with all 37 outcomes, found all round-1 points resolved and no place where the claims file misreads the paper, so no question was added for a reader. It asked for wording fixes in the fig2efgh, fig5ab, ed8 and fig4ac (README) conclusions, and found that the units with out-of-order spike times are 11, not 13, and that the record's example inversion was not printed. The notebook now prints the units with out-of-order spike times (11 of 29) with the first inversion of each segment, and the cell count, the example (2399.4923 s after 2399.4926 s) and the largest inversion (0.7 ms) are corrected in the notebook, Summary and finding. No outcome changed and none is proposed. Report in transcripts/mohebi-2019/verifier-2-report.md.

entries.name: mohebi-2019
entries.title: Dopamine cell firing in the bandit and Pavlovian tasks (Mohebi et al. 2019)
entries.description: Tests the dopamine cell findings of Mohebi, Pettibone, Hamid, Wong, Vinson, Patriarchi, Tian, Kennedy and Berke (2019) on CRCNS data set vta-2, which holds the spike times of the 29 optogenetically identified VTA-l dopamine cells with their bandit, Pavlovian and laser segments. It tests motivation and reward rate, the identification and firing rates of the cells, their Pavlovian responses, tonic firing across reward blocks, cue responses, approach ramps and reward prediction error coding. The microdialysis, photometry, histology and untagged units of the paper are not in the data set.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Mohebi et al. (2019) from CRCNS vta-2
